opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think we have to be careful about inferring competence from performance on the kinds of tests we happen to give these systems. When a human passes a medical licensing exam, we make a lot of assumptions about what else that person can do, because we know how humans learn and how their knowledge is structured. Those assumptions don't transfer to a system trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next word.

A good illustration comes from Go. The top Go programs were thought to be superhuman, far beyond any human player. But researchers found that you could beat them, even with a fairly amateur player, by building a particular kind of large circular group. The programs simply don't understand the basic concept of a group of stones and whether it's alive or dead. They had learned an enormous number of patterns that let them play brilliantly in typical positions, but they never acquired the underlying concept that any decent human player has. So the appearance of mastery was masking a fundamental gap.

I suspect something similar is going on with large language models. Part of the reason is the representational form. A circuit, which is essentially what these networks are, is a very poor way to represent general concepts like "a group of connected stones" or the rules of arithmetic. You end up with a huge patchwork of special cases that approximates the concept in the regions where there's a lot of training data, and then falls apart outside them. That's also why these systems need so much data, orders of magnitude more than a human child, to reach a given level of performance.

And we've seen this repeatedly: models that can do arithmetic on numbers of a certain length but fail on slightly longer ones, or that answer a question correctly and then contradict themselves when it's rephrased. That's not what you'd expect from something that actually has a model of the world it's reasoning about.

So I'm not saying they're not impressive. They are extraordinary in many ways. But "impressive output" and "humanlike understanding" are different things, and we really don't know what's going on inside these systems. That uncertainty matters a great deal when we're talking about deploying them widely, or about how close we are to general-purpose AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that performance and understanding are two different things, and we've been conflating them for a long time. When a system produces the right answer, we're tempted to infer that it got there the way a human would, with some internal model of what's going on. But the history of AI is full of cases where that inference turns out to be wrong.

Take chess or Go. These programs play at a superhuman level, and yet they have no idea that they're playing a game, no idea that there's an opponent, no notion of what it means to win except as a number that gets maximized. We don't say Deep Blue understood chess. We say it was very good at chess. And I think the same caution applies to the large language models, only it's harder to maintain because the output is in English, and English is the thing we use to detect understanding in other people. So all our intuitive instruments are being fooled.

What's actually happening, as far as we can tell, is that these systems have absorbed an enormous amount of text and have become extraordinarily good at predicting what text comes next. That's a remarkable achievement. But it means that when you ask a question, you're often getting back a kind of weighted average of what humans have said in similar contexts, not the result of the system reasoning from a model of the world. And you can see the seams. You ask a question that's phrased slightly differently from how it appears in the training data, and the performance falls apart. You give it a problem that requires keeping track of a few objects and their relationships over several steps, and it loses the thread. A child who understood the situation wouldn't make those errors, because the child's answer is anchored to the situation rather than to the words.

There's also a deeper issue, which is that we don't know what's going on inside. With a chess program, I can read the code and tell you exactly why it made a move. With these systems, we have a trillion parameters and essentially no theory of how they produce their outputs. So when someone claims humanlike understanding, I'd ask: on what basis? Not on the basis of looking inside, because nobody can. It's purely on the basis of behavior, and behavior that's been selected, quite literally, to resemble human output. That's a very weak form of evidence.

I should be careful here. I'm not saying these systems are trivial, and I'm not saying they'll never have something we'd want to call understanding. I'm saying that the burden of proof is on the people making the strong claim, and that right now the evidence consists mostly of being impressed. And being impressed is something we've been before, in 1960, in 1985, in 1997, and each time the thing we were impressed by turned out to be narrower than it looked. So I'd rather we do the hard work of actually figuring out what these systems can and can't do, and why, rather than reaching for a word like "understanding" that mainly reflects our own psychology.

astra-6.text:
Because the same outward performance can arise from very different underlying processes. A system can produce a convincing answer without arriving at it in anything like the way a person would. So we have to be careful about moving from “it does this task very well” to “it understands what it’s doing.”

Think about a chess program. It can beat you decisively, but that doesn’t establish that it understands chess in the human sense, let alone that it knows it’s playing a game. Its competence is real; the interpretation we put on that competence is a separate question.

With language, this becomes particularly difficult because language is how we normally recognize understanding in other people. When something speaks fluently, we naturally attribute beliefs, intentions, and a grasp of the world to it. But fluency alone doesn’t tell us whether those attributions are justified. We need to investigate whether its understanding holds up when the situation changes, whether it can distinguish causes from correlations, and whether its answers reflect a consistent model of the world. Impressive performance is evidence to examine, not a reason to stop asking those questions.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, because performance is something we can observe, whereas understanding is a hypothesis about what produces that performance. And we have to be careful not to confuse the two. A system can produce an excellent answer without arriving at it in anything like the way a human would.

Think about chess. A program can play far better than any human, but that doesn’t mean it thinks about chess as we do, let alone understands anything outside the game. With language, we’re more susceptible to making that inference because language is how we usually recognize intelligence in other people. If something speaks fluently, we naturally imagine a mind behind the words.

That doesn’t establish that there’s no understanding there. It means fluency alone doesn’t settle the question. We need to ask whether the system has a coherent account of the world, whether it can use what it has learned in unfamiliar circumstances, and whether its answers remain sensible when we change the assumptions. Impressive performance is evidence of a capability. It isn’t, by itself, an explanation of that capability.
